title: Before your condo board signs a repair contract: how to check a contractor's Florida license and insurance
seoTitle: Florida Condo Boards: Check a Contractor's License
description: How a Florida condo board or owner can check a contractor's license and workers' comp on free state sites, and what happens if it's unlicensed.
dek: It takes a few minutes and two free state websites. Here is what to look up, what the results mean, and what Florida law says happens when a contractor turns out to be unlicensed.
facebook: Your board is about to sign a big repair contract. Did anyone look the contractor up? Two free state websites show whether a Florida contractor is licensed and carries workers' comp. Here's how to check, and what the law says if the license isn't there.

Florida contractor workers comp proof of coverage

body.text: Many Florida condo buildings have big repair work ahead: concrete, roofs, balconies, waterproofing. Before any of that starts, a board signs a contract. One of the simplest things a board can do first is look up the contractor on the state's own websites.
Owners can do the same check. The records are public and free. Here is what to look up, what Florida law says, and who to ask when something does not look right. It is a guide, not legal advice.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: DBPR: the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, the state agency that licenses contractors. Certified contractor: holds a state license good anywhere in Florida. Registered contractor: holds a state registration based on a local license, good only in the city or county where it was issued. Qualifying agent: the licensed person a contracting company must have on file with the state. Workers' comp: insurance that pays for a worker's injuries on the job. Lien: a legal claim against property for unpaid work.
What condo law already requires

Florida's condo law, section 718.3026 of the 2026 Florida Statutes, says contracts for services must be in writing. If a contract will cost more than 5 percent of the association's total annual budget, including reserves, the association must get competitive bids. That means more than one price for the same work.

The law also says the association does not have to accept the lowest bid. There are exceptions. Contracts for attorneys, accountants, architects, engineers, landscape architects, community association managers and association employees are not covered by this section. Neither is a true emergency, or a business that is the only source of supply in the county. Associations with 10 or fewer units can opt out if two-thirds of the owners vote to do so.
The condo law does not spell out a license check. But bids are the natural moment to do one, because Florida's contractor law requires the license number to be on the bid itself.
Step 1: Find the license number on the bid

Section 489.119 says a contractor's registration or certification number must appear in each offer of services, business proposal, bid, contract and advertisement. It must also go on every building permit application. DBPR's unlicensed activity program lists a missing license number as a red flag: "If you can't find it, verify it—or walk away."
Step 2: Look it up on DBPR

DBPR's Verify a License search at myfloridalicense.com lets anyone look up a license by name or license number. There is also a DBPR mobile app. If you would rather call, the Customer Contact Center is (850) 487-1395.

When you look, check three things. Does the name on the license match the company on the bid? Is the license active? And is it a certified license, good anywhere in Florida, or a registered one, good only where it was issued? Section 489.105 says registered contractors may contract only in the jurisdiction where their registration was issued.
Step 3: Check workers' comp

The Florida Department of Financial Services runs the workers' comp system. Its coverage page says construction employers with one or more employees must carry workers' comp, and that owners who are corporate officers or LLC members count toward that number. The department has two free search tools: a Proof of Coverage database, which shows whether a business has a policy on file, and an Exemption Search, which shows officers who have opted themselves out.

Contractors swear to the state that they carry workers' comp, liability and property damage insurance when they get or renew a license, under section 489.115. That is a sworn statement at renewal time, not proof the policy is active today. That is why boards often ask for a certificate of insurance and call the agent listed on it to confirm.
What the law says if a contractor is unlicensed

items: The contract can't be enforced by that contractor. Section 489.128 says a contract entered into by an unlicensed contractor is unenforceable by the contractor, and no lien or bond claim exists in the contractor's favor.

What counts as unlicensed. A person is unlicensed if they lack a license the law requires. A company is unlicensed if it has no qualifying agent. The check is made as of the contract's effective date, or the first day of work if no date is given.
It is a crime. Under section 489.127, unlicensed contracting is a first-degree misdemeanor. During a state of emergency declared by the Governor, it is a third-degree felony.

The $2,500 exemption is narrow. Section 489.103 exempts casual, minor work under $2,500 total. It does not apply if the job is part of a larger project, if the work is split up to stay under the limit, or if the person advertises as a contractor.

body.text: Unenforceable does not mean the problem goes away. DBPR's program warns that unlicensed work can mean paying twice to redo it, lost deposits, failed inspections and permit problems. In fiscal year 2024–25, the program received 2,830 construction complaints.
What to do
If you are an owner:

items: When a board agenda lists a contract, ask in writing for the contractor's name and license number. Look it up yourself before the meeting.
Ask whether the board got more than one bid if the job is more than 5 percent of the total annual budget.
Bids and contracts are official association records. Section 718.111 says bids must be kept for at least a year after they arrive. If you want to read them, ask in writing.

body.text: If you are on the board:

items: Make the license check part of every bid review. Print or save the DBPR result with the bid.
Check workers' comp on the state's Proof of Coverage database, and ask for a certificate of insurance. Ask your association attorney what coverage and limits the contract should require.
Watch for DBPR's red flags: pressure to sign now, a large payment up front, no written contract, no license number, or "we don't need a permit."
If something looks wrong, call DBPR's Unlicensed Activity Hotline at (866) 532-1440 or email ULA@myfloridalicense.com. For questions about the contract itself, ask the association attorney.

faq.q: How do I check if a contractor is licensed in Florida?
faq.a: Use DBPR's free Verify a License search at myfloridalicense.com and search by name or license number, or call DBPR's Customer Contact Center at (850) 487-1395. Check that the name matches, the license is active, and whether it is certified (statewide) or registered (local only).

faq.q: Does a Florida condo board have to get competitive bids?
faq.a: Yes, for contracts that cost more than 5 percent of the association's total annual budget, including reserves, under section 718.3026. The board does not have to pick the lowest bid. Some services, such as attorneys and engineers, true emergencies, and sole-source suppliers are exempt.

faq.q: What happens if a condo association hires an unlicensed contractor in Florida?
faq.a: Under section 489.128, the unlicensed contractor cannot enforce the contract and has no lien or bond claim. Unlicensed contracting is also a crime under section 489.127. Ask the association attorney about the association's options.

faq.q: How can I check if a Florida contractor has workers' comp?
faq.a: The Florida Department of Financial Services has a free Proof of Coverage database and an Exemption Search. Construction employers with one or more employees must carry workers' comp, and owners who are corporate officers or LLC members count toward that number.

faq.q: Does a handyman need a license for small condo repairs in Florida?
faq.a: Florida exempts casual, minor work under $2,500 total. The exemption does not apply if the job is part of a larger project, if it is split up to stay under $2,500, or if the person advertises as a contractor.
